263.text: The key efficiency win: the target model scores ALL drafted positions in ONE forward pass. Autoregressive decoding would need K separate forward passes. Since inference is memory-bound (reading weights dominates), one pass costs almost the same as K.

285.text: The denominator of alpha. Counting here rather than at the top of the loop is what keeps alpha the literature's per-token acceptance rate: tokens that were never examined never dilute it.

286.text: The acceptance probability: min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If the target likes this token at least as much as the draft, always accept. If the target likes it less, accept proportionally. This ratio is what guarantees the output distribution matches the target exactly.

288.text: Coin flip: accept with the computed probability.

290.text: Token accepted, add to the final sequence.

291.text: Bump the accepted token counter. We'll compare accepted vs. drafted to compute the acceptance rate.

292.text: Special case: accepted token is BOS (end of sequence).

293.text: Remove BOS from the output and stop generating.

298.text: The BOS was verified and accepted, so it counts in accepted even though it is popped off and never emitted. accepted measures verification outcomes, not output length, which is why the earlier "don't count BOS" behaviour was wrong for alpha.

303.text: The residual distribution, and the most subtle line in the lab. Clamping p - q at zero keeps only the mass the target wants that the draft under-supplied; resampling from that (normalized) exactly compensates for the tokens the accept test rejected. This clamp plus the min(1, p/q) test above is the whole losslessness proof of Leviathan et al.

304.text: Sum the corrected distribution to check if it has positive mass. If it's all zeros, we'll fall back to the raw target distribution.

305.text: If there's positive mass in the adjusted distribution...

306.text: Normalize to a proper probability distribution.

308.text: Fallback: if adjustment zeroes everything out, use the target's raw distribution.

434.text: The arbitrage the whole technique depends on. At this scale the cost ratio and the parameter ratio have come apart completely, because both models are dominated by per-call Python and dispatch overhead rather than arithmetic. In production that ratio is 10-100x, which is where the reported 2-3x speedups come from.

439.text: The wall clock, reported as a ratio rather than a "speedup" because on this box it comes out below 1.00. Printing an unflattering measurement is the point: the forward-pass reduction is real and transfers, the wall clock is a property of this CPU and this interpreter.
